dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Read problem.py, kernel.py, run_tests.sh, submission_tests.py in full; correctly extracted opcodes, slot limits, per-bundle cost model, SIMD width (VLEN=8), SCRATCH_SIZE, and the forest/rounds/hash-stage computation before editing.
Built quantitative machine model: valu_min=ops/6, load_min=ops/2; correctly diagnosed load vs valu as bottleneck across D_OPT settings, tying counts to a theoretical cycle floor.
Probed ambiguous simulator behavior with targeted experiments: pause/enable_pause semantics, within-bundle WAR hazard timing by reading the simulator's end-of-cycle effect model, and vload behavior.
Per-cycle profiling of load/valu slot fill to locate idle load regions and underfilled valu cycles; re-probed to understand what limited parallelism (dependency chains, hash critical path).
When a correctness bug surprised it, traced the exact offending op and cycle through the simulator to find idx_v corruption — orientation continuously refined as optimization exposed new unknowns.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read problem.py and the reference kernel in full and correctly extracted ops, slot limits, cost model, and computation (well beyond the level-5 bar), then built an explicit quantitative model of the machine with dependency chains, slot contention, and a theoretical cycle floor (level 8), and continuously re-probed the simulator with small experiments whenever behavior surprised it (level 10 traits). It falls just short of a perfect 10 because it assumed uniform 1-cycle op latency rather than deriving explicit instruction latencies, placing it at a strong 9.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates

evidence.note: Clear opening stage: understood the batch-vectorization opportunity, wrote a correct from-scratch vectorized rewrite, and measured it (2331 cycles, correctness passing) before optimizing — a genuine 'correct baseline → vectorize → checkpoint' milestone.

Explicitly computes per-configuration min-cycle bounds (valu min vs load min) and uses which one dominates to decide the next transform — evidence-driven re-prioritization of the decomposition rather than a fixed plan.

Each transform (D_OPT sweeps, round-14 broadcast, dispatch changes) is landed, measured, and reverted when it regresses; backups kernel_v1/v2/v3 make every step independently revertible — strong per-change measurement discipline.

Mid-trajectory becomes a somewhat undifferentiated stream of scheduler-heuristic and op-reordering attempts, each tried one at a time with little planned staging — no explicit milestone hierarchy or per-stage cycle budget toward 1250.

Late reflection acknowledges the plan is bottlenecked by loads/gather and questions whether the whole approach is limited, but never restructures into new budgeted milestones; wraps up at 1753 without a planned software-pipeline stage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly staged the opening (correct vectorized baseline → measure → bottleneck-driven optimization) and kept every transform independently measurable, revertible, and grounded in recomputed valu/load min bounds — exceeding the level-5 'sensible ordered plan with rough targets.' But it never laid out an explicit milestone hierarchy with per-stage done-checks and cycle budgets; after the baseline the work becomes a long stream of one-at-a-time micro-optimizations and reactive scheduler tweaks rather than sequenced planned stages, falling short of the level-8 clear-milestone structure. This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test

evidence.note: Runs run_tests.sh to confirm correctness+cycles; consciously decides run_tests.sh (which uses randomized inputs) is the authoritative correctness check after local test breaks on pause handling.
After WAR-dependency removal breaks correctness, reasons explicitly about VLIW WAR/WAW hazards and stale-register semantics — a guard against a scheduling-specific corruption mode.
Builds custom trace scripts to diff scratch values op-by-op, isolating the exact stale-lane subtraction bug (cycle 1164) that the canonical test flagged; disciplined but reactive debugging.
Re-runs run_tests.sh after the idx_off change to confirm correctness preserved and compares valu counts; verifies final instrs structure compliance before submit.
Repeatedly runs run_tests.sh after broadcast-dispatch experiments, catching N_CAND sizing errors before trusting the transform.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently runs run_tests.sh after significant/risky changes, confirming both correctness and cycles and re-checking at each optimization stage (anchor 5), and it relies on the provided randomized-input tests knowingly. It exceeds a pure canonical-pass mindset by building custom trace/diff scripts and reasoning about VLIW-specific WAR/WAW corruption to isolate broken transforms (touching anchor 8/10 behaviors). But these additional checks are reactive diagnostics triggered by test failures rather than a proactive regime of self-constructed edge inputs and per-transform isolation, and not every semantic change got a fresh correctness run — placing it at a 6, between anchors 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection

evidence.note: Continuous, accurate cycle ledger with per-change deltas (2331→1936→1887→1837→1742), each attributed to a specific transform — clear transform→delta tracking.
Repeatedly computes theoretical floors (valu-min 1510, load-min 1315) and states exact distance to target/slack, distinguishing 'done enough' from remaining headroom deliberately.
Explicitly recognizes plateaus ('stuck at 1783', 'wall', schedule 'essentially deterministic') and knows it passes test_75x but not the 1500/1250 targets.

Grinds by re-running the D_OPT sweep many times across the trajectory, and re-attempts the idx_off optimization 3+ times (122-128,171-207) despite it never reducing cycles — thrash on exhausted approaches.
Multiple scheduler-heuristic experiments all yielding 'Same'/'worse'; agent notices they don't help but keeps trying variants, indicating partial rather than decisive redirection.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a clear, accurate transform→cycle-delta ledger with theoretical bounds and continuously reconciles measured cycles against the 1250/1500 targets, which places it well above the level-5 anchor and squarely into level-8 territory on tracking and distance-awareness. It also recognizes plateaus explicitly. But it falls short of a clean 8/10 because it repeatedly grinds on exhausted approaches (D_OPT sweeps, idx_off retries, scheduler heuristics) rather than decisively redirecting — the exact 'circling' the dimension warns about — so I place it at 7.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead

evidence.note: When XOR-stage reduction and D_OPT sweeps (1,2,3) failed to help or regressed, the agent measured each, recognized the change was worse ('D_OPT=3 worse'), and reverted to the better setting rather than persisting on the falsified idea.

Repeated scheduler-heuristic experiments (critical-path, FIFO, ALAP, engine-prio, tie-break-by-vector) each gave 'same' or worse; agent reverted each and eventually updated its model ('the schedule is essentially deterministic given dependencies'), redirecting away from scheduler tweaks. Some mild circling here.
WAR-removal broke correctness and round-14 broadcast regressed cycles; in each case the agent backed the change out cleanly and returned to the known-good 1783/1753 state.

Genuine cost-model correction on surprises: noted valu went UP yet cycles went DOWN (scheduler packs better), and later that saving 318 valu ops did NOT cut cycles because the region was load-bound — updating the load-vs-valu bottleneck model rather than assuming the prediction held.

The idx_off transform broke correctness multiple times; agent deep-debugged (traced u32 underflow to a missing is_off flag), fixed it, then found it saved valu but not cycles and reverted cleanly to kernel_safe. Preserved hard-won state via kernel_v1/v2/v3/safe backups throughout (steps 84,131,154,171).

Recognized the sub-1500 wall was structural (load floor ~1280) but never actually pivoted the whole gather-based strategy despite repeatedly musing about VLOAD; kept revisiting the same tactic — the main gap versus the level-10 anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently treats falsified predictions as signals to revise its cost model and reverts cleanly, disciplined by explicit backup copies of known-good states (matching the level-8 anchor: clean reverts, diagnosis of why expectations were wrong, avoiding entrenchment). It repeatedly diagnosed the valu-vs-load bottleneck distinction and corrected its machine model (pause behavior, WAR, scheduler determinism). It falls short of 9-10 because it never pivots the whole gather strategy despite recognizing the structural load floor, shows some flailing across near-identical scheduler heuristics, and re-attempts idx_off after it had already failed once.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget

evidence.note: Early derivation of theoretical floors: load bottleneck (2 slots/cycle, mem-read count), valu floor (ops/6), identifying loads as dominant consumer and quantifying savings from the idx=0 broadcast specialization (255 fewer loads = ~127 cycles/round).
Sustained max(valu_min, load_min) cost model with explicit slack tracking (e.g. valu=11327/6=1888 vs load=1100; 'valu is bottleneck, 200 over'), used to decide next optimization target.

Repeatedly recomputes floors as ops change (valu 9031/6=1505, load 2691/2=1346), reasons about D_OPT crossover where valu vs load becomes binding, and notes reducing valu 'doesn't help when load-bound'.

Per-cycle slot-occupancy profiling: quantifies valu fill (4.25/6 in load-bound gather regions), locates 155 idle-load cycles (1330-1485), attributes ~278-cycle slack to dependency chains rather than op count.
Critical-path modeling: identifies vec 31's serial hash chain finishing at cycle 1750 as the tail limiter, distinguishing latency from throughput bounds.

Final recognition of the fundamental gather floor: 2560 scalar loads/2 = 1280 cycles min, concluding <1250 is near-impossible with this architecture without a vload-gather breakthrough — recognizing near-optimality relative to the achievable bound.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently built an explicit quantitative model tying instruction counts and per-slot occupancy to cycles (valu_ops/6, loads/2, max as floor), estimated theoretical lower bounds, and used the measured-vs-floor gap plus critical-path analysis (vec 31 hash chain) to decide which transforms were worth attempting — matching anchor 8 and reaching into anchor 10 by ultimately deriving the gather floor (~1280) and recognizing the kernel was near the achievable bound. It falls just short of a clean 10 because the decisive load-gather floor was only crystallized at the very end after substantial trial-and-error scheduler/D_OPT tuning rather than being used up front to prune the search.

rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
